name: Heightmaxxing 3-level guide

lead: The heightmaxxing 3-level guide is a community format that ranks height-related methods in tiers: natural habits at the base, non-surgical aids in the middle, and surgery at the top. Versions differ between authors, but the common idea is to order options by invasiveness and cost.

The payoff is a taller standing frame or a taller-looking one: habits and posture work toward reaching or showing one's full natural height, lifts add height while worn, and limb lengthening surgery adds real bone length.

paras: In descriptions of this tiering, the first level covers nutrition, sleep and posture (relevant mainly while still growing, and for presenting full height afterwards). The middle level covers things like hidden shoe lifts and insoles, which add height inside the shoe while worn. The final level is cosmetic limb lengthening, an orthopedic procedure with a long recovery.

Habit-level methods carry little risk. Shoe lifts can change gait comfort. Limb lengthening is major surgery with reported infection, hardware failure, nerve injury and under-delivery of expected height, and it has been restricted or banned in some places.

chain: Habits: nutrition, sleep and posture support reaching and showing full natural height
Aids: hidden lifts add height while worn
Surgery: limb lengthening adds bone length
angle.text: The guide organizes methods by how much height they can add and how invasive they are. The first tier supports natural stature and posture, the second adds height inside the shoe, and the third changes bone length surgically.

lead: The 'heightmaxxing 3-level guide' is a community framework for ordering the ways people try to be, or look, taller. Versions circulate in looksmaxxing forums with differing details; the shared structure is a ladder from natural habits to external aids to surgery.

Genetics largely set adult height: twin studies put heritability at roughly 60 to 80 percent, and nutrition and health in childhood and adolescence also shape it, with growth in boys typically ending around 18 to 19 [1]. This is why tiers aimed at natural growth are usually framed around reaching one's potential rather than exceeding it.

Stature added after growth ends comes from the upper tiers: elevator shoes, which hide a thickened heel section inside the shoe so the wearer looks taller [2], and limb lengthening, in which a cut bone is gradually separated, at about a millimeter per day in common protocols, while new bone forms in the gap [3].

paras: Accounts of the guide differ, but the layers are consistent: lowest cost and risk first, surgery last. The first tier is natural: adequate nutrition, which strongly influences height in childhood and adolescence, and posture, since measured height also varies through the day by about 1.5 cm in one reported study [1].
The second tier is external. Elevator shoes place a thickened insole section under the heel so the wearer appears taller without the visible platform of high heels [2].

The third tier is limb lengthening (distraction osteogenesis), in which a bone is cut, fitted with an external or implanted device, and slowly lengthened before a consolidation period and, for some devices, removal surgery [3].

Reported complications of limb lengthening include infection (about 5 percent overall), bone not growing in the intended direction, hardware failure and nerve injury [3]. Cosmetic demand is high in India, where height is associated with marriage and career prospects; reported problems include procedures on very young patients, extra surgeries and less height gained than expected, and China's health ministry banned the procedure in 2006 [3]. Ilizarov's work from the 1950s underlies modern practice [3].
No studies found on the tier framework itself. Research on the individual tiers exists in the broader literature on human growth and limb lengthening [1][3].

timeline.event: Bernhard von Langenbeck proposes limb lengthening [3].
Alessandro Codivilla publishes the first clinical lengthening efforts [3].
Gavriil Ilizarov begins the work that leads to widespread use of distraction osteogenesis [3].
China's Ministry of Health bans limb lengthening [3].
